brief.what_it_is: Simple Event Correlator (SEC) is a lightweight event correlator, per its SourceForge page: a tool for network management, log file monitoring, security management, fraud detection, and other tasks that involve event correlation. It is listed as a non-interactive daemon written in Perl, and the Homebrew formula installs an executable named sec. The homepage did not say in plain words what it takes in or emits, so that detail is unconfirmed. Its scout note describes it as a Perl rule engine for chaining logs and events.
brief.why_it_exists: The homepage gives no problem statement beyond the one-line description: event correlation for network management, log monitoring, security and fraud detection.
brief.install_notes: Nothing beyond the Homebrew formula name (sec) was visible on the homepage. The SourceForge listing names Perl as the programming language, so a Perl runtime is implied, but no install steps, configuration, or first-run instructions appeared in what I fetched.

I fetched only the homepage and did not follow the optional extra links, so the commands list is empty and how it works is unexplained. The license is GNU GPL version 2.0. entry.title: sec
entry.tldr: Simple Event Correlator, a Perl daemon that watches event streams like logs and applies rules to spot patterns across them.
entry.deeper_look:
SEC describes itself as "a lightweight event correlator for network management, log file monitoring, security management, fraud detection, and other tasks which involve event correlation." It is a non-interactive daemon written in Perl, and Homebrew installs it as a single executable named `sec`.

The idea underneath is event correlation: one log line rarely means much, but a particular sequence, a repeat count, or a missing follow-up within a time window can. Tools like this turn a stream of raw messages into a smaller number of meaningful events. That is a door into how monitoring and security systems reason about logs.

The project has been registered on SourceForge since 2001, so it is old. The brief did not cover how rules are written or what the tool reads and emits, so those details are for the project's own documentation to answer.
entry.install:
brew install sec
# Perl is implied by the project listing; the brief did not confirm install steps or first-run configuration.
